concept.name: Citation traceability
concept.definition: The property of a knowledge system that every asserted claim can be traced back, through its provenance records, to the specific source document and location that supports it. It operationalizes the attribution and derivation relations of provenance models such as W3C PROV at the granularity of individual claims.
concept.intuition: No orphan claims: for every statement the system makes, you can click through to the exact document, page, or section it rests on and verify it yourself.
concept.mechanics: Each claim stored or generated by the system carries a citation object (source identifier, URL, section, access date); validation checks that citations resolve to real, fetched documents, and review workflows re-verify that the source text actually supports the claim. Derived claims inherit and compose the provenance of their inputs.
concept.failure_modes: Breaks when citations are fabricated or point to real documents that do not support the claim (a known failure of LLM-generated references), when sources change or disappear after citation, or when claims blend multiple sources but cite only one.
concept.misconceptions: A plausible-looking citation is not traceability — the citation must resolve to a fetched source whose content genuinely supports the claim. Traceability also does not make a claim true; it makes it checkable.
concept.example: This library requires every reviewed entry to carry {source, url, section, accessed}; a reviewer re-fetches the URL and confirms the definition follows from the cited text before promoting the entry's trust status.

citations.source: W3C, 'PROV-Overview: An Overview of the PROV Family of Documents' (W3C Working Group Note, 2013)
citations.section: Section 1 (attribution and derivation as core provenance concepts)
